content: 1. Health facilities must establish systems to ensure that adolescents are well-informed about their own health and are aware of where and when to access health services. 2. Health facilities should implement systems that engage parents, guardians, community members, and organizations to recognize the importance of providing health services to adolescents and to support their utilization of these services. 3. Health facilities must offer a comprehensive package of services, including information, counseling, diagnostics, treatment, and care, tailored to meet the diverse needs of all adolescents. These services should be accessible both within the facility and through referrals, linkages, and outreach programs. 4. Health-care providers must demonstrate the technical competence necessary to deliver effective health services to adolescents. Providers and support staff must respect and uphold adolescents' rights to information, privacy, confidentiality, non-discrimination, non-judgmental attitudes, and dignity. 5. Health facilities should maintain convenient operating hours, a welcoming and clean environment, and ensure privacy and confidentiality. They must also be equipped with the necessary tools, medicines, supplies, and technology to provide effective services to adolescents. 6. Health facilities must deliver quality services to all adolescents, regardless of their ability to pay, age, sex, marital status, education level, ethnicity, sexual orientation, or other characteristics. 7. Health facilities should collect, analyze, and utilize data on service usage and quality of care, disaggregated by age and sex, to support continuous quality improvement. Staff should be supported to engage in ongoing quality improvement efforts. 8. Adolescents should actively participate in the planning, monitoring, and evaluation of health services, as well as in decisions about their own care and relevant aspects of service provision. 9. Research should focus on understanding how to implement adolescent-friendly health services at a programmatic level and assess the cost-effectiveness of these approaches, particularly in HIV services in lowand middle-income countries. 10. Research on adolescents living with HIV should explore the minimum package of care, delivery models at various service levels (including for key populations and pregnant adolescents), integration of sexual and reproductive health (SRH) into antiretroviral therapy (ART) services, safe disclosure interventions, treatment literacy, mental health interventions, and the impact of provider training and peer interventions. 11. HIV care programs should adopt quality assurance (QA) and quality improvement (QI) practices to enhance service delivery. These practices should be integrated into daily activities at all levels, from service delivery to national program management. 12. People-centered health services should prioritize the perspectives of individuals, families, and communities, treating them as active participants in trusted health systems that respond to their needs and preferences in a humane and holistic manner. 13. Integrated health services should ensure a continuum of care, including health promotion, disease prevention, diagnosis, treatment, disease management, rehabilitation, and palliative care, across all levels and sites of care within the health system. 14. HIV programs should provide people-centered care that respects individual dignity, particularly for vulnerable populations, and supports individuals and families in making informed decisions about their care. 15. HIV programs should offer safe, acceptable, and timely clinical and non-clinical services to reduce HIV-related morbidity and mortality, improve health outcomes, and enhance quality of life. 16. National HIV programs should plan for a phased adoption of new recommendations, such as expanding ART to all people living with HIV and introducing pre-exposure prophylaxis (PrEP) for high-risk groups, while ensuring adequate resources and avoiding stock-outs or imbalances. 17. Procurement and supply management (PSM) systems must ensure the continuous availability of effective, quality-assured antiretroviral drugs, diagnostics, and consumables at service delivery sites in the right quantities, at the lowest cost, and in a timely manner. 18. Stakeholders, including networks of people living with HIV, communities, and health-care workers, should be involved in strengthening the quality of HIV care services and ensuring efficient resource use. 19. National policies and strategies should address the quality of HIV care services, reduce HIV-related stigma, and prioritize QA and QI strategies. 20. HIV programs should define roles and responsibilities for stakeholders at different levels of the health-care system to strengthen the quality of HIV care services and allocate resources for mechanisms that support QI. 21. High-quality, people-centered HIV care should be included in national policies and strategic plans, with standards set for evidence-based care and defined packages of services for specific populations and geographic locations. 22. Lessons from QI processes in HIV care should inform subsequent policy and program planning to ensure sustained improvement in service delivery. 23. Comprehensive quality-of-care activities should include both QA and QI efforts, with a focus on continuous monitoring and improvement of HIV care services.
